datasets.target_description: acceleration a = dv/dt (paper: v-dot), CSV column 'a' (last column)
datasets.split: Fixed published files cut from one simulated trajectory (scipy solve_ivp from x = 0.5, v = 0.5 over the time range (0, 50); App. D.1 pp. 19-20, Table 2), sampled at t_k = 50 k / 49999 (k = 0..49999): train.csv (10,000 rows) holds the odd samples with t in (30, 50]; test_id.csv (10,000 rows) the even samples with t in [30, 50), so each in-domain test row lies between two training rows of the same stretch of time; test_ood.csv (10,000 rows) the even samples with t in [0, 20), the out-of-domain test (App. D.1 p. 20: 'we utilize the time interval T = [0, 20) to evaluate the out-of-domain generalization'). The samples with t in [20, 30) and the odd samples with t in [0, 20) are in no file. The paper says only that the data are split by trajectory time and that [0, 20) is out-of-domain; the sample positions were read by integrating the printed law again (RK45, rtol 1e-10): every row lies within 4.2e-07 of the re-integrated trajectory at its sample. The file has no t column; each row's sample was found by its nearest point on the re-integrated trajectory. No row is shared between files. Raw values, no scaling (main.py l.43 reads data/<problem>/train.csv; the last column is the target).
datasets.seeds: None needed and none published: the data are one deterministic simulation; the authors publish no generator script and do not state the integrator's tolerances (the files agree with a tight re-integration to 4e-7, not with scipy's defaults, which miss by up to 3e-3).

datasets.formula_as_published: \dot{v} = F \sin(\omega x) -\alpha v^3 - \beta x^3 -\gamma x \cdot v - x \cos(x)
datasets.formula_as_published_note: LaTeX verbatim from the arXiv v3 source (sections/appendix.tex, App. D.1 p. 19; the same law in Sec. 3.1 p. 6), with the constants of Table 2 p. 19 ('Parameter values for Oscillator datasets'): F = 0.8, omega = 1.0, alpha = 0.5, beta = 0.2, gamma = 0.5.
datasets.notes: The paper prints the law and every constant: the formula is the printed law with Table 2's values (omega = 1.0 is written as sin(x)); nothing is fitted. It reproduces the target of every row of all three files to max abs error 3.5e-16 (FVU <= 9.81e-31): the files are noise-free, and the target is the law evaluated at the stored inputs, not a numerical derivative. The rows are points of one trajectory, not independent draws: x and v move together, and the training rows trace one curve in the (x, v) plane, about 1.1 turns around the origin, so laws that differ off that curve can fit them equally well. llm-sr-oscillators.notes: KIND data: the authors' fixed train/test_id/test_ood files of the two nonlinear oscillators of LLM-SR (Shojaee et al., ICLR 2025). Framed as second-order ODEs, v-dot = f(x, v) and v-dot = f(t, x, v), but each file is a table of the inputs with the derivative a = dv/dt as its target column, the law evaluated exactly at every row, so each problem is ordinary y = f(x) regression on one data set (a published derivative table). The paper prints both laws (Sec. 3.1 p. 6; App. D.1 p. 19) and all their constants (Table 2 p. 19), so the ground truth is the printed law with the printed values, and it reproduces every row of all six files to max abs error 2.6e-15 (FVU <= 1.73e-30): the files are noise-free. Each oscillator is one simulated trajectory from x = 0.5, v = 0.5: training rows and in-domain test rows alternate along its last 20 s (t in [30, 50]), the out-of-domain test is its first 20 s (t in [0, 20), larger amplitude), and t in [20, 30) is in no file (read from the files by integrating the printed laws again; the paper states only the [0, 20) out-of-domain interval). As in the sibling LLM-SR sets, each dataset is fitted on train.csv and tested once on test_id.csv (in-domain) and once on test_ood.csv (out-of-domain), two problems per oscillator. The rows lie on one curve per oscillator, so the inputs are not independent: the in-domain test interpolates along the curve, and laws that differ off the curve fit the training rows equally well. The authors' point counts (10,000 per file) and their noise (none) are information only; srbf draws at most 512 fitting and 512 test rows per run and sets the noise.

bms-rossler.notes: DATA set of 6 problems, one per derivative (xdot, ydot, zdot) and noise level (sd 1, sd 5): inputs the states x, y, z, target one noisy derivative. Ground truth: the Rössler right-hand sides with the authors' constants a = b = 0.2, c = 5.7 (Fig. 4; Text S4 Eqs. 5-7). The authors published no data for this experiment: not in rguimera/machine-scientist (pinned commit 9defb7a, every branch head including no_degeneracy at f4cf1e8, and every one of its 224 commits: no Rössler file and no mention in any file), not in the supplementary files (the PDF, figures and a movie); the paper says additional data may be requested from the authors. The supplement's Figs. S4 and S5 embed the authors' matplotlib figures as vectors, which fixes the run exactly: 1,000 points at t = 0, 0.1, ..., 99.9; the first state is (0, 0, 0.0002), one forward-Euler step of 0.001 from the origin; forward Euler with step 0.001, every 100th step, reproduces the true-model curves of both figures to <= 3e-7 at every plotted vertex, while an accurate ODE solution from the same start departs by up to 31 in zdot. The figures also give the authors' own noisy ydot and zdot at sd 5 (1,000 markers each, recovered to ~1e-7; Figs. S4 and S5 agree on zdot to 1.3e-7); with these, srbf's fits reproduce the BIC values printed in Text S4 (true model 6133.53 vs 6133.5, most plausible model 6127.89 vs 6127.9). The noisy xdot at sd 5 and all three derivatives at sd 1 were never published: srbf draws their noise once with a fixed seed. The authors sample 10,000 models per series on all 1,000 points: no split. The trajectory is a transient spiralling out of the inner fixed point (within 0.1 of it until t ~ 10 and within 1 until t ~ 35: 347 of the 1,000 rows), not a sample of the attractor. Every law leaves one state unused (x in xdot, z in ydot, y in zdot). srbf runs only the two series whose values are the authors' own (ydot and zdot at noise sd 5, recovered from the vector data of Supplementary Figs. S4-S5); the other four were never published.

settings.right_hand_side_as_coded: dx/dt = sigma*(y - x), dy/dt = x*(rho - z) - y, dz/dt = x*y - beta*z
settings.integrator: scipy.integrate.solve_ivp, method RK45 (Dormand-Prince 5(4)), rtol 1e-3, atol 1e-6 (the defaults; the notebooks pass no tolerances), dense output at t_eval
settings.rows: inputs = all state variables at the t_eval points; target = this state's right-hand side evaluated at those states (the notebooks: rhs([0], solution.y)[k])
settings.notebook: Notebooks/PySR_pipeline.ipynb cells 10, 21, 22 (identical in the GPLearn, AI Feynman, PyKAN, ODEFormer and random-forest notebooks; PySINDy's uses step 0.002)
settings.paper: Sec. III A 1 and Table VI (sigma = 2.0, rho = 1.0, beta = 2.6; x0 = 0.6, y0 = 2.0, z0 = 1.0; window [0, 5], step 2E-3). The notebooks use step 0.02 (250 rows), except PySINDy's, which uses the 2E-3 of the table (2,500 rows, for its finite differences). Sec. III A 1 prints dy/dt = -x(rho - z) - y; the notebooks and the paper's results Table III use x(rho - z) - y = x(1 - z) - y. At rho = 1 the system is not chaotic: the trajectory relaxes towards the origin.

datasets.split: none: the authors fit each derivative on all rows of its trajectory and score the found equation on the same rows (MAE, MSE, R2, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Sec. IV C and the notebooks' error_eval). Method-specific splits exist but define no benchmark test: PyKAN trains on the first 80% of the rows and tests on the last 20% (train_test_split(test_size=0.2, shuffle=False)), the random-forest baseline on a shuffled 75/25 split (random_state=42), and AI Feynman splits internally.
datasets.notes: Lorenz system, dx/dt; one of 3 regressions on the same 250 solved states (x is shared by the system's problems). brum-2025.notes: DATA set of 28 problems: the nine ODE systems Brum, Lober, Previdelli & Rodrigues benchmark symbolic regression on (Lorenz, nonlinear pendulum, Lotka-Volterra; SIS, SIR, SIRV, SIRS, SEIR, SEIRD), one regression per state variable: all states of the system as inputs, that state's right-hand side at the solved states as the target, the form in which GPLearn, AI Feynman, PySR, PyKAN and the random-forest baseline receive the data (PySINDy differentiates the same trajectories numerically, ODEFormer reads the trajectories). Like SRBench's Strogatz set, the targets are exact derivatives at simulated states. The paper gives the benchmark no name; the slug is taken from its title. The authors publish no data files: the rows exist only inside their notebooks (https://github.com/luizalober/review_symb_regression @ 094bd15, 'Reviewed codes for arxiv v2 and JP:C publication' 2026-01-19 plus a README update), which solve each system with scipy's solve_ivp (RK45, default tolerances) on np.arange(0, t_end, t_step). srbf regenerates them with its own code from those settings. Settings follow the notebooks where the paper's Tables VI-VII differ (Lorenz step 0.02 not 2E-3; pendulum window [0, 10) and step 0.01 not [0, 5] and 2E-3; Lotka-Volterra predator coefficient d*b = 0.1875 not delta = 0.375; SIRV I0 = 0.1, S0 = 0.85, rate 0.2 not 0.01, 0.94, 0.5): the notebooks made the rows, and their stored outputs confirm the coded values (PySR recovers 0.1875*u*v and -0.5*S*I - 0.2*S). Where the notebooks differ among themselves (PySINDy's Lorenz step 0.002; GPLearn and PySINDy pendulum g = 9.81; PyKAN's pendulum initial state swapped; AI Feynman and random-forest SEIR and SEIRD trajectories solved with gamma = 1.0), srbf follows the PySR and ODEFormer notebooks, whose settings the majority of notebooks shares for every system. The extra SINDy_pipeline notebook (not one of the paper's methods) uses other rates and is not used. Compartments are fractions (N = 1): they sum to 1 on every row (within 7e-16), so an epidemic derivative is fixed only up to that identity (on the rows -0.3*S*I + 0.1*I equals -0.2*S*I + 0.1*I**2, the form PySR and AI Feynman return for SIS), and SEIRD's recovered and deceased columns are identical (gamma = mu). Noise study (Sec. V A, Fig. 5): Lotka-Volterra and SIR with Gaussian noise of 1, 5 and 10% of each series' standard deviation added to every state and target, drawn from numpy's global random state (np.random.seed(100) at the top of each notebook, then consumed by whatever ran before; the cells' execution counts are cleared), separately in each method's notebook; those 15 noisy problems cannot be regenerated and are not run. No split (see datasets[].split). The integrator: scipy's own RK45 forms its stage sums with BLAS, whose kernels round differently on different CPUs (the authors' notebooks themselves were run on two machines whose rows differ in the last bits), so srbf's generator writes the same algorithm out with every sum in a fixed order: identical bytes on any machine, equal to scipy's output where BLAS sums in plain order, and within rounding of it elsewhere (see verification).
